chapter_title: Advanced Load Balancing and Auto Scaling for Performance

screens.title: Advanced Load Balancing and Auto Scaling for Performance
screens.subtitle: Choosing and tuning ALBs, NLBs, and ASGs to meet high-throughput, low-latency requirements

narration.text: In this chapter we focus on two core building blocks for high-performance networked systems: the Application Load Balancer and the Network Load Balancer, and how Auto Scaling Groups can be driven by network metrics to preserve performance under load. You will learn to distinguish the design trade-offs: ALBs bring Layer 7 routing and request awareness, which helps microservices and path-based routing, while NLBs operate at Layer 4 for extreme throughput and ultra-low latency. We’ll explore health checks and target groups so backends are only sent traffic when truly ready, and we’ll discuss the real cost implication of cross-zone traffic, especially for NLBs. A concrete example you will see later is a target-tracking policy that uses average NetworkOut to trigger scale-out when outbound network usage approaches a capacity threshold. Throughout, I’ll highlight common misconceptions — for example, assuming ALB is always better because it has more features, or that disabling cross-zone load balancing always reduces cost without other trade-offs. By the end you will be able to select the right balancer, tune health checks and target groups, and design ASGs that react to network pressure while managing cost.

Second, you will optimize basic load balancer configurations such as target group health checks and connection settings to reduce latency and avoid unhealthy-instance thrashing. screens.title: ALB vs NLB — Protocols and Performance
screens.subtitle: When to use Layer 7 routing versus Layer 4 forwarding

narration.text: Start with a clear definition. The Application Load Balancer is a Layer 7 device that understands HTTP and HTTPS. It can inspect host headers, paths, and query strings and apply routing rules. The Network Load Balancer operates at Layer 4, forwarding TCP, UDP or TLS streams with minimal processing for the lowest possible latency. A concrete example: a containerized microservices platform serving many distinct URL paths benefits from ALB’s path-based routing, while a multiplayer game server that needs consistent sub-10 millisecond latency will favor an NLB. A common misconception is to assume the balancer with more features is always better; in fact, more processing adds latency and can reduce throughput. Another contrast: ALBs natively integrate features like sticky sessions and WAF, which are useful for web apps, while NLBs preserve client IPs and scale to millions of connections per second when throughput matters. Practical rule of thumb: if you need HTTP-level routing and inspection, choose ALB; if you need raw speed and connection preservation, choose NLB. Reflect: which of your services needs intelligent routing versus predictable, minimal latency? ALB vs NLB — Protocols and Performance means choose alb for http routing and features; choose nlb for raw tcp/udp performance and client ip preservation.. In practical terms, when to use layer 7 routing versus layer 4 forwarding. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Match balancer to workload

content.html:
Core Concept
ALB vs NLB
Decide by protocol needs and acceptable latency.
Application Load Balancer (ALB)
  • Layer 7 routing: host/path/query rules.
  • Sticky sessions, WAF integration, request-based routing.
  • Best for microservices, web apps, and containers.
Network Load Balancer (NLB)
  • Layer 4 forwarding: TCP/UDP/TLS with minimal processing.
  • Ultra-low latency and very high throughput.
  • Preserves client IP; useful for gaming, IoT, and performance-critical backends.
Key Takeaway

Select the balancer by protocol and latency needs: ALB for HTTP features, NLB for raw connection performance.

Concrete examples and misconception
Example: A microservice using path-based routing should use ALB so you can route /api, /static, and /admin differently. Example: A multiplayer game handling raw TCP connections should use NLB for consistent low latency. Misconception: Choosing ALB solely because it has more features can add latency; measure whether features are necessary.
When to pick ALB
Routing by host/path, WAF protection, content-based routing.
When to pick NLB
High throughput TCP/UDP services, static IPs, client IP preservation.
Reflect: Which services in your environment need request-level routing versus raw connection speed?

screens.title: Target Groups and Health Checks
screens.subtitle: Ensuring only ready targets receive traffic

narration.text: First, define a target group: it is a logical collection of targets—EC2 instances, IPs, or Lambda functions—that a load balancer uses to route traffic. Health checks are the mechanism the load balancer uses to determine whether a target is healthy and able to receive requests. A robust health check tests application readiness rather than only network connectivity. For example, a TCP health check that returns success when the port accepts a connection may still allow traffic to an instance that cannot process requests due to an internal error. A better health check could be an HTTP endpoint that exercises a downstream dependency and returns success only when the full request path works. One common mistake is setting overly aggressive health check intervals and low thresholds, causing transient failures to remove targets too quickly and trigger unnecessary scaling or failover. Another mistake is setting checks that are too lax, keeping unhealthy targets in rotation. Key practical advice: tailor intervals and thresholds to your application’s startup and recovery characteristics and consider custom endpoints that assert real readiness. What endpoint would best represent true readiness for your service?

keyIdea.title: Test real readiness
keyIdea.text: Use health checks that verify application-level correctness, not just port availability, and tune intervals to your application’s behavior.

content.html:
Definition
Target Groups & Health Checks
Make sure only healthy targets receive traffic.
Target Group
A named set of targets that the load balancer forwards requests to. Targets can be instances, IPs, or serverless endpoints.
Health Check types
HTTP/HTTPS checks validate app responses; TCP checks validate port availability. Use HTTP checks for readiness when possible.
Key Takeaway

Design health checks that exercise the same code paths your users hit, and tune intervals and thresholds to avoid flapping.

Example health check
Use GET /health which checks DB connectivity and downstream caches; return 200 only when ready to serve traffic.
Common Mistake
Relying on a simple TCP check that does not validate the application’s ability to process requests.
Pro Tip
If startup time is long, increase healthy threshold or startup delay to avoid premature removal during boot.

screens.title: Optimizing ALB Configuration for Throughput and Latency
screens.subtitle: Health checks, keepalives, and target distribution best practices

narration.text: To optimize an Application Load Balancer for both throughput and reasonable latency, follow a few systematic steps. First, design health checks that capture application readiness — choose an endpoint that verifies essential downstream services. Second, set reasonable intervals and healthy/unhealthy thresholds: too aggressive may cause flapping and too lax may keep degraded targets in rotation. Third, enable connection-level tuning such as keepalive timeouts on back-end servers to avoid extra TCP handshakes under steady traffic. Fourth, ensure targets are evenly registered across multiple Availability Zones and that each zone has sufficient healthy capacity. A concrete example: if your microservice needs 10 seconds to warm up, set health-check grace and healthy thresholds so the ALB waits for readiness rather than removing the instance. A common misconception is that shorter health-check intervals always improve responsiveness; in practice they can cause oscillation and increased C P U from repeated checks. Final step: monitor RequestCountPerTarget and backend latency metrics to validate the configuration. How would you adjust intervals if you observe occasional flapping during deployments? Optimizing ALB Configuration for Throughput and Latency means adjust health-check intervals, connection timeouts, and az distribution to match your application startup and steady-state behavior.. In practical terms, health checks, keepalives, and target distribution best practices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Tune for behavior, not defaults
keyIdea.text: Adjust health-check intervals, connection timeouts, and AZ distribution to match your application startup and steady-state behavior.

content.html:
Process Flow
ALB Optimization Steps
  1. Design readiness checks. Use endpoints that verify essential dependencies.
  2. Set intervals thoughtfully. Match checks to startup and recovery times.
  3. Tune keepalives and timeouts. Reduce handshakes for persistent traffic.
  4. Distribute targets across AZs. Ensure capacity per zone to avoid hotspots.
  5. Monitor and iterate. Use RequestCountPerTarget and latency metrics to refine settings.
Key Takeaway

Defaults are a starting point; match checks and timeouts to real application behavior to avoid instability.

Concrete example
If a service needs a cold-start time of around 10 seconds, set your health-check grace and healthy thresholds accordingly rather than relying on very short intervals. This prevents the ALB from marking the instance unhealthy during boot.
Misconception
Shorter intervals always improve availability. In reality, overly frequent checks can create load and false failures.
Check: After a deployment, if you see flapping, increase healthy thresholds or add a startup grace period for checks.

screens.title: NLB Configuration for Ultra-Low Latency
screens.subtitle: Keep throughput high while preserving client IPs

narration.text: The Network Load Balancer is designed to pass traffic with minimal processing. Define its role clearly: forward TCP, UDP, or TLS streams while preserving client IPs when required. A concrete example from the chapter: gaming servers or IoT backends use NLBs because they need predictable, ultra-low latency. For NLBs, health checks can be TCP or HTTP/HTTPS; TCP checks simply ensure the backend port accepts connections, while HTTP checks can be used when the backend serves HTTP over TCP. A common operational pitfall is assuming AWS cross-zone behavior is identical for all balancers. While cross-zone is enabled by default for both ALB and NLB, NLB cross-zone traffic can incur data transfer charges, so turning it off reduces cross-AZ data transfer but risks uneven load if AZ capacities differ. Practical tuning advice: ensure your target distribution per AZ matches expected traffic, enable TLS termination at the target if you need inspectability, and monitor connection rates per target. Final reflection: where in your workload would preserving the client IP be essential, and what cost trade-offs might that require? NLB Configuration for Ultra-Low Latency means use nlb to preserve client ips and handle very high connection rates; evaluate cross-zone costs when distributing targets across azs.. In practical terms, keep throughput high while preserving client ips. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NLB for speed and transparency
keyIdea.text: Use NLB to preserve client IPs and handle very high connection rates; evaluate cross-zone costs when distributing targets across AZs.

content.html:
Core Concept
Network Load Balancer (NLB)
Minimal processing for extreme throughput.
  • Operates at Layer 4: TCP, UDP, TLS.
  • Preserves client IP addresses for backend visibility.
  • Handles millions of requests per second when needed.
Cross-zone behavior & example
NLB cross-zone is enabled by default but may incur cross-AZ data transfer charges. If you disable cross-zone balancing, traffic is only routed to targets in the same Availability Zone as the client’s connection, which can lower transfer costs but can create uneven distribution if AZ target counts differ.
Operational tip
If you must disable cross-zone, ensure each AZ has balanced capacity and health checks to avoid hotspots.
Key Takeaway

NLBs minimize latency and preserve IPs; balance cross-zone cost decisions with availability and even target counts across AZs.

screens.title: ASG Target Tracking on NetworkOut — Policy Example
screens.subtitle: A concrete Auto Scaling policy using ASGAverageNetworkOut

narration.text: Let’s walk through a concrete target-tracking policy that uses an Auto Scaling predefined metric for average NetworkOut. The policy aims to keep the fleet’s average outbound network throughput near a desired target so instances aren’t saturated. In the example you will see a policy named ScaleOutOnNetworkOut that references ASGAverageNetworkOut and sets a target value. One concrete detail: the policy in the chapter uses a TargetValue of 80.0 in a JSON example, which represents 80 percent in that context; another hands-on example sets a numerical byte target like 8,000,000 for bytes per second. Both approaches illustrate that you can use either percent-based or absolute metrics depending on the metric type. A common misconception is to rely solely on C P U for scaling when the bottleneck is network bandwidth; this leads to instances that are C P U-light but network-saturated. When you implement this, monitor CloudWatch NetworkOut and RequestCountPerTarget to validate that scaling occurs before network saturation. How will you choose the target value for your instance type’s expected network capacity? ASG Target Tracking on NetworkOut — Policy Example means use asgaveragenetworkout or a custom network metric to scale when network i/o, not cpu, is the limiting factor.. In practical terms, a concrete auto scaling policy using asgaveragenetworkout. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scale on the right metric
keyIdea.text: Use ASGAverageNetworkOut or a custom network metric to scale when network I/O, not CPU, is the limiting factor.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Auto Scaling Policy Example
A target-tracking policy using ASGAverageNetworkOut.
{
  "PolicyName": "ScaleOutOnNetworkOut",
  "ScalingTargetId": "arn:aws:autoscaling:region:account:autoScalingGroup:my-asg",
  "TargetTrackingConfiguration": {
    "PredefinedMetricSpecification": {
      "PredefinedMetricType": "ASGAverageNetworkOut"
    },
    "TargetValue": 80.0,
    "DisableScaleIn": false
  }
}
Notes: TargetValue can be percent-like or an absolute byte value depending on metric. Monitor NetworkOut in CloudWatch and choose a target that avoids consistently hitting 100% of expected capacity.
Concrete use
Set a policy so the ASG launches new instances before network bandwidth reaches critical levels.
Common Mistake
Scaling only on CPU while NetworkOut is saturated leads to continuing network bottlenecks despite more CPU availability.
Check your math
Choose a target based on instance network capability and expected per-instance throughput so scaling triggers at the right moment.

screens.title: Cross-Zone Load Balancing — Performance and Cost
screens.subtitle: How cross-AZ routing affects distribution and data transfer costs

narration.text: Cross-zone load balancing determines whether a load balancer will route requests to targets in other Availability Zones. For ALB, cross-zone balancing is enabled by default and is free. For NLBs, cross-zone balancing is also enabled by default but the chapter warns that cross-zone traffic may incur data transfer charges. A concrete scenario: three AZs each with one instance, and a user connects to the balancer endpoint in AZ-A; with cross-zone enabled, the request might be sent to an instance in AZ-B or AZ-C, which could cause inter-AZ data transfer. If you disable cross-zone balancing on an NLB, traffic only goes to targets in the same AZ as the client connection, which can reduce cross-AZ transfer cost but may create uneven load if AZ capacities differ. Many teams mistakenly disable cross-zone without ensuring balanced targets per AZ; that can overload an AZ with insufficient capacity. The decision therefore depends on your cost sensitivity and whether you can maintain balanced capacity across AZs. What monitoring signals would tell you cross-zone disabling is harming performance? Cross-Zone Load Balancing — Performance and Cost means enable or disable cross-zone load balancing based on whether reducing cross-az transfer costs outweighs the risk of uneven target distribution.. In practical terms, how cross-az routing affects distribution and data transfer costs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Balance cost vs. distribution
keyIdea.text: Enable or disable cross-zone load balancing based on whether reducing cross-AZ transfer costs outweighs the risk of uneven target distribution.

content.html:
Comparison
Cross-Zone Load Balancing
Weigh even distribution against potential data-transfer costs.
ALB
Cross-zone enabled by default and free. Distributes requests evenly across registered targets regardless of AZ.
NLB
Cross-zone enabled by default but cross-AZ traffic may incur charges. Disabling keeps traffic within the connection AZ.
Concrete example and checks
If cost is a major concern and you have AZ-local high availability patterns, disabling NLB cross-zone can reduce inter-AZ transfer costs. But monitor per-AZ request distribution and target utilization. If one AZ’s targets are overloaded while others are idle, re-enable cross-zone or rebalance capacity.
Misconception
Turning off cross-zone automatically saves money with no trade-offs. In reality, you must confirm even AZ capacity to avoid performance regressions.
Key Takeaway

Decide cross-zone settings based on both cost and how well you can keep AZ capacity balanced under load.

screens.title: Designing ASGs for Network-Intensive Workloads
screens.subtitle: Capacity planning, metrics selection, and scaling sensitivity

narration.text: Designing Auto Scaling Groups for network-heavy workloads requires choosing the right metric and planning capacity sensitivity. First, capacity planning: estimate per-instance network capability and decide how many concurrent flows or bytes per second a single instance should handle. Second, metric selection: prefer ASGAverageNetworkOut or a custom RequestCountPerTarget from an ALB if your traffic is request-oriented. Third, scaling sensitivity: select target values and cooldowns so the ASG scales before saturation but avoids flapping. As a concrete example, if an m5. large typically sustains a certain bytes-per-second level under your workload, set TargetValue so the average approaches but does not exceed that level. A typical mistake is using short cooldowns and aggressive targets that cause repeated launches and terminations. Another pitfall is ignoring request distribution; use RequestCountPerTarget when ALB is fronting many short-lived requests. Finally, validate with sustained tests and review ASG activity and CloudWatch alarms to refine thresholds. Which metric best reflects your real bottleneck: network bytes or requests per target? Designing ASGs for Network-Intensive Workloads means estimate per-instance network capacity, choose a network-aware metric, and tune targets and cooldowns to avoid thrashing while preventing saturation.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Architecture
ASG Design for Network Workloads
Pick metrics and sensitivity that reflect network constraints.
Estimate per-instance bytes/sec capacity and set target accordingly.
Use ASGAverageNetworkOut or RequestCountPerTarget depending on request model.
Tune cooldowns and target values to avoid oscillation.
Key Takeaway

Align the scaling metric with the real bottleneck and validate with sustained load tests before finalizing targets.

Concrete scenario
If instances show low CPU but high NetworkOut, switching scaling to ASGAverageNetworkOut prevents adding CPU-bound instances that don’t relieve the network bottleneck.
Common Mistake
Relying only on CPU utilization for network-bound services leads to persistent network saturation despite more instances.

screens.title: Testing and Monitoring Scale Behavior
screens.subtitle: Generate traffic, observe CloudWatch metrics, and iterate

narration.text: Validating your configuration is as important as setting it correctly. Begin by planning a traffic pattern: sustained outbound transfers or continuous request streams that match real workload behavior. For example, using iperf3 or serving large files will exercise NetworkOut. While tests run, monitor CloudWatch metrics: NetworkOut, NetworkIn, RequestCountPerTarget, and ALB/NLB target-level latencies. Watch ASG activity history to see scale events and the timestamps when instances launch and become healthy. A common pitfall is using short spike tests that trigger transient scaling but don’t reveal steady-state behavior. Instead, run longer tests long enough for the ASG to scale and for new instances to register healthy. If the ASG scales but request latency remains high, consider that the new instances may be suffering from cold-start or misconfigured health checks. Always iterate: adjust target values, cooldowns, and health-check settings, then retest. Which metric would tell you that the ASG responded early enough to prevent saturation? Testing and Monitoring Scale Behavior means use sustained traffic tests and monitor network and request metrics to verify scaling prevents saturation and preserves performance.. In practical terms, generate traffic, observe cloudwatch metrics, and iterate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Remediation Checklist
screens.subtitle: A compact checklist to avoid performance regressions

narration.text: Here is a practical checklist to catch common issues that harm performance. First, verify health checks exercise true readiness; update endpoints if they only test a port. Second, confirm targets are registered and healthy across multiple Availability Zones and that each AZ has sufficient capacity to avoid hotspots. Third, ensure your scaling metric reflects the bottleneck: use network metrics when network is constrained, not just C P U. Fourth, review cross-zone settings for NLBs if you see unexpected data transfer costs. Fifth, validate that keepalive and connection timeout settings align with your traffic patterns. A frequent error is treating defaults as optimal: health-check intervals, target thresholds, and cooldowns should reflect your application. After running tests, inspect CloudWatch for sustained NetworkOut, RequestCountPerTarget, and ASG history entries that indicate whether scaling acted early enough. Use this checklist as a remediation plan: adjust one parameter, retest, and iterate until results are stable. Which single change would you test first in your environment?   • Prefer network metrics for network-bound services.
  • Set realistic TargetValue and cooldowns.
Work through changes one at a time, rerun sustained tests, and confirm metrics stabilize before making further adjustments.

narration.text: These key concepts summarize the chapter’s essential definitions. Application Load Balancer is a Layer 7 balancer that routes HTTP and HTTPS traffic using host and path rules, useful when request-level decisions are needed. Network Load Balancer is a Layer 4 balancer that forwards TCP/UDP/TLS traffic with minimal processing, preserving client IP and enabling very high throughput. Target Group is a logical collection of targets—instances, IPs, or functions—that a load balancer routes to, and health checks determine whether targets are eligible to receive traffic. Keep these core ideas in mind as you make design choices. Key Concepts — Set 1 means remember what alb, nlb, and target groups are and why each exists..
